source.title: Semantic Tube Prediction: Beating LLM Data Efficiency with JEPA
source.authors: Hai Huang; Yann LeCun; Randall Balestriero

record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly argues that its fine-tuning data-efficiency results challenge the data term of scaling laws. However, those experiments do not measure the power-law loss, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation specified in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. but does not reproduce their scaling measurements. Its own experiments vary fine-tuning dataset size and report task accuracy, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fitted scaling curves. The reported data-efficiency outcomes are recorded as findings related to the claim's subject, but do not measure any listed version. Other fine-tuning benchmark results, regular-expression suffix results, and loss-landscape results do not test a listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper frames its results as challenging the Chinchilla data term, but its experiments only compare its own fine-tuning regularizer (STP) with regular fine-tuning on task accuracy across data fractions. It fits no power law, extrapolates nothing, measures no pretraining loss, and runs no compute-optimal search. Showing that a new objective needs less data does not bear on whether loss follows a power law in data. That would at most shift a constant, and no version claims data efficiency cannot be improved. The scaling-law discussion is framing, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that STP lets models keep accuracy with 1/16 of the fine-tuning data on NL-RX-SYNTH. They present this as 'directly violating the data term of Chinchilla-style scaling laws' and argue that scaling laws describe typical rather than optimal training. The paraphrase should add that this is a single-dataset fine-tuning result with no fitted scaling curve.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces a fine-tuning regularizer and compares task accuracy across dataset fractions; it does not apply the original scaling-law measurement and fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported task accuracy varies with dataset fraction and training configuration; the paper also varies compute, learning rate, and the STP weight λ. These are fine-tuning settings, not tested scaling-law fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: For Llama-3 1B, STP fine-tuning shows a negligible accuracy drop at 1/2 data and matches full-data regular fine-tuning at 1/16 data. Regular fine-tuning drops significantly at 1/2 data. The paper says 3B and 8B show a similar trend (Fig. 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An auxiliary geometric regularizer (STP) improves fine-tuning data efficiency relative to next-token-prediction fine-tuning.

record.problems: The evidence is fine-tuning task accuracy on NL-RX-SYNTH rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fitted scaling curves. Exact values for the dataset-fraction comparisons are only in figures; the text gives the 1B-level qualitative summary and says the 3B and 8B trends are similar. The reported experiments use five seeds, but uncertainty for the plotted comparisons is not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 1 and 12 show additional dataset fractions and compute/training-setting variants. Their separate plotted values are not extracted because the text does not give those values or clearly specify every plotted comparison. Other benchmark accuracy results, the suffix-diversity table, and the fine-tuning loss-landscape results do not measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured against parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fit.
No fit on small runs and no extrapolation to larger runs.
No shape or architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
Fine-tuning accuracy is reported across data fractions, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.
Accuracy is reported for 1B, 3B and 8B models, but predictability with scale or loss is not tested.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The claimed violation of Chinchilla scaling is rhetorical. Chinchilla concerns pretraining loss against tokens and parameters, not fine-tuning accuracy on a small task dataset under a modified objective. Epochs were scaled n× for a 1/n data fraction, so the reduced-data runs repeat data many times, which further separates this setup from scaling-law regimes. All values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep across parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power-law fit on small runs or comparison with larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
No controlled architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
The study fine-tunes language models, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in fine-tuning or another training regime.
It reports task accuracy, but does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices, and no test of whether scaling curves bend.
